subject: elephant
pitch: A gentle African elephant calf. Wrinkly slate-grey skin with a dusty, reddish tint from rolling in the dirt, huge fan-shaped ears with a pink flush on the inside, a curious trunk curling forward, stubby baby tusks, long lashes over kind brown eyes, a little tufted tail and round, padded feet with pale toenails.
reasoning:
I'm planning a single TypeScript module built with the SDK, combining chains, sweeps, joints, extrusions for the ears, sprouts for tusks, and decals for the eyes, with painted mottling for texture. I'll scale it to roughly the size of a real African elephant calf for proportion reference.

Now I'm sketching the skeleton: a hips joint as the root around y=0.95, a spine chain running from the rump to the shoulders via catmull points, and a neck chain leading up to a separate head joint, naming each segment so the structure stays organized.

The neck chain can parent directly off the spine chain's final joint, running from around the shoulder area up to a tip named "head." For the torso itself, I'm thinking of sweeping a barrel-like shape along a centerline path from rump to shoulder, binding it to the hips/spine joints, with radius varying by parameter to give it a belly-ish profile.

I'll use a loft with station points defining width and height along the body, skinned to the hips and spine chain. Then for legs, I'm planning four pillar-like limbs placed at the front and rear corners, using limb() with segment lengths roughly matching an elephant's proportions—shoulder to elbow, elbow to wrist, wrist to foot.

For the two-bone IK legs, I'm computing lengths and root/target positions so the distance stays within reach, settling on root hip height 0.85 and foot height 0.1 with segment lengths [0.4, 0.38] for a slight natural bend, and I'm giving front and hind legs opposite bend directions to mimic columnar elephant legs. I'm now setting up the chain to name the joints shoulder, elbow, and foot for each leg.

I'm mirroring left/right legs by flipping the x offset sign and suffixing names with L or R, and now I'm working out the ear geometry -- extruding a fan-shaped outline positioned on the side of the head, figuring out which local axes correspond to forward, up, and outward-thickness directions so the ears flap naturally away from the skull.

I'll place the ear as a part attached to the head joint using the extrude `at` point so it inherits the bone correctly, using directional words like left/up/back with signed values to handle left/right symmetry. For the trunk, I'm planning a chain of joints following a catmull curve that sweeps down from the face and curls upward at the tip.

For the trunk geometry itself, I'm defining the curve points so it dips forward and down from the head before curling back up near the tip, then setting up a chain parented to the head joint with four segments. I'll sweep the trunk with a tapering radius from a thicker base to a narrower tip, and I'm considering adding mottled wrinkle texture to the skin surface.

For ear coloring, I'm using a paint function that checks whether a face's normal points toward the midline (inner side) versus outward, so I can color the inside pink and the outside slate depending on which ear side it's on.

For eyes, I'm adding a dark brown sphere with a small white catchlight highlight, plus eyelashes created using a ring of spikes arranged around the eye along an outward-facing direction, following the SDK's ring/spike pattern for lash placement.

Checking the highlight placement sits properly on the eye's outward surface, then working through the head joint's orientation to confirm which local axis points forward given the neck's tangent direction.

For the head itself, I'm shaping it as a slightly scaled sphere attached at the head joint, then positioning the ears laterally on the sides using mirrored placement. For the tusks, I'll sprout them from a surface hit point on the head mesh near the mouth front, defining tip position and radius.

Working out the trunk's path coordinates, starting from the head's front-bottom and curving downward then curling upward at the tip, so it reads as a natural elephant trunk shape.

Now I'm working out the tail, chaining it from the hips with a curving path and tapering sweep, then adding a tuft of small spike shapes near the tip for texture.

Still defining the skeleton...

Simplifying: head joint parented directly to the neck chain, positioned slightly forward and up with a direction pointing forward-and-up. Now I'm moving on to the trunk, which parents off the head joint's position.

Still defining ear geometry...

For the body, I'll use a mottled slate-and-dust material shared across all painted parts, keeping legs the same tone for visual consistency.

Now I'm working out foot placement: rounded padded cylinders positioned so their centers align with where the leg targets end, letting the bottom rest at ground level and the top meet the ankle joint smoothly.

For toenails, I'm adding four small flattened cylinders spaced across the front-bottom of each foot, colored pale, sitting just barely above ground level to avoid clipping.

Now I'm working out the leg IK chains: front legs get a shoulder root with a two-segment reach down to the ground, bending forward with a single direction vector applied to the inner joint, and I'm starting on the hind leg root position similarly.

I'm sweeping tapered radii along each leg chain for thickness, rooting the hip/shoulder joints inside the body mesh so they blend with the torso loft, and naming the joints per side (shoulder/elbow/foot, left/right) for each leg chain.

I'm adding eyelash spikes ringed around the eye frame, picking brown/white/lash color values for the small eye spheres, and sprouting ivory tusks from the nearest point on the head surface.

I'm now working out the sprout tip positions and radii for the tusks so they emerge near the trunk base pointing forward and down, placing them just left and right of the trunk, then checking the ear attachment point and setting up a dark brown spiky tuft ring at the tail tip.

For the tail, I'm using a ring of outward-pointing spikes at the tip to create a brush-like tuft, and sweeping the tail itself in a reddish skin tone. For body texture, I'm considering adding wrinkle detail by mixing two colors based on a noise function to break up the flat skin tone.

Instead of risky color mixing, I decide to use a mottle paint for the base skin pattern combined with a scales effect layered on top, since scales draws outlined cells that can double as wrinkled skin plates—nesting the mottle paint as the base color and a darker crease tone for the edges.

Now I'm working out the body structure: lofting the torso along spine and hip bones, then building the spine chain as a catmull curve with two joints parented to the hips joint, making sure the chain's start position matches the hips location so everything connects properly before setting up the neck chain off the spine's last joint.

Continuing, I'm defining the neck chain as a curve ending at a head joint, sweeping it with appropriate radii to match a thick elephant-calf neck, then placing the head sphere centered on that head joint with a slight scale adjustment so it blends smoothly into the neck.

I'm now positioning the eyes and ears relative to the head using local offsets, placing small spheres for eyes angled slightly outward and forward, sized to fit just within the head's surface.

Checking the overall proportions next: head height, body loft, and leg lengths line up reasonably for an elephant calf shape, so I move on to adding eye lashes and planning the final code structure.

I'm sketching out the imports needed from the builder module, defining color constants like slate and dust tones, and preparing to write the spike function for lashes.

With the palette set, I work out how to layer skin texture using scaled mottling, then plan the ear paint logic to blend pink interiors with the scaled skin tone on the outside, confirming the paint callback receives a proper normal vector for directional blending. Writing module imports...

Still writing module structure...

Adding paw pads and toenail geometry...

Positioning the toenail disc right at the foot's front surface, roughly z=0.4, so it sits flush against the curved foot shape rather than floating.

Now moving to the tail, I'm building a short chain off the hips with a few catmull-rom points curving down and back, then sweeping skin-colored geometry along it and adding a ring of small spike tufts near the tip for texture.

For the trunk, I'm chaining it off the head with a longer catmull-rom curve and sweeping a tapered skin tube along it, though I'm second-guessing which "role" tag best fits a trunk since it's not quite a tail or a limb.

Now I'm detailing the head geometry with a scaled sphere, then placing the eyes symmetrically using local head-space offsets and directional vectors, adding tiny white highlight spheres on each eye, and ringing small lash spikes around the eye edges within a defined angular range.

Shifting to the ear shape, I'm building an extruded fan-like outline that attaches near the top-front of the head and extends backward and downward, with thickness, bevel, and a color function that paints the inner edge pink versus skin-toned elsewhere.

Now I'm sprouting the tusks from the head sphere using a nearest-point attachment and a target tip position angled forward, down, and outward, keeping them short and ivory-colored for a calf-appropriate stubby look.

I'm verifying the trunk and tusk positions sit coherently relative to the head sphere and each other, then confirming the surface hit computation finds the right nearest attachment point. I still need to export the meta object with name and description, double-check the mottled skin paint scales call, confirm the spine bone chain parented to the hips joint, and make sure every constant like SKIN is actually used.

I'm now defining the hind leg limbs symmetrically using the side coordinate, checking that their joint names like hipL/kneeL/footL don't collide with the hips root joint, and verifying the mesh count looks reasonable before writing out the final answer.
